4.1 Heeling During Turning - The maximum angle of heel of all selfpropelled ing at service speed with maximum loading shall not exceed 10".

vessels

during

turn-

4.1.1 The heel angle shall not exceed 6" while stationary or plying in fair weather conditions for Groups A, E and F; and in case of Group D vessels when there is maximum pull on the towing hook ( up to an angle of 60' off centreline of vessel ). In case of Group B vessels, heel angle shall not exceed 3" or an angle as specified by the manufacturer with maximum load on hook and at maximum designed outreach of boom of crane or garb. height ( in metres ) shall 4.2 Metacentric Height - The metacentric services; however, it shall, in any case, be not less than 0'15 m. 4.3 The metacentric height shall be calculated for at least 3 different indicated in 5, 5.1, 5.1.1 and 5.2 for Groups A, 6, C, D and G vessels. shall, in addition, be shown hopper spoils of 2 or 3 different specific carrying vessels with two more different cargo stowage rates. 4.4 Freeboard 4.5 Stability ( F ) Data Minimum freeboard as per statutory to stability requirements are given be adequate for intended

EXPLANATORY

NOTE

An attempt has been made in this standard to lay down guidelines for stability for inland and harbour crafts, Some requirements such as heeling are somewhat common in some form or the other especially heeling during turning at service speed in most of the vessels. But Indian harbour vessels are so varied in type that it is di~cult to stipulate minimum GMt. However, an attempt has been made to put down the common requirements in a simplified form. These are mainly based on the limit ranges of KIW and KG for different types of vessels having L/B up to 4"5 and B/T = 4 to 5, when range of draught is from 0"75 to 1"8 m. Mostly, while designing, the lower limits are taken. However, precautions are required to be taken when the vessels become stiff. Thus, Upper limit of GA6 may be as high as B/4 � 0"25 m, At present, there are rules available which govern stability of such crafts though they vary from port to port depending upon local requirements; but a common set of rules can also satisty almost all conditions. It is a fact that maximum casualty takes place because of insufficient stability in passenger vessel. Suticient practical Precautions for safety are required to be taken, An attempt has been made in this standard towards this direction. Not withstanding what is stated in the standard, the rules and requirements statutory authorities, as applicable in all respect, shall apply. This standard is being issued in the following two parts: laid down by the
